The supplied text had several garbled/cut-off fragments (mid-sentence corruption, likely a copy-paste glitch, same pattern as prior weeks' scripts) -- repaired to complete sentences preserving the evident intended meaning; every repair is logged verbatim in FACTCHECK.md. metadata.description: The theory behind canary and blue-green deployments: the shared problem both solve (a standard deploy exposes 100% of users instantly), how a canary gradually ramps traffic while monitoring, how blue-green validates a fully isolated second environment before an atomic cutover, why Cloud Run's immutable-revision-plus-traffic-percentage model makes both just two usage patterns of one primitive rather than separate features, how to choose between them, and why deployment strategy is risk management, not just automation.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- Claude cream skin, slide 1 title card
beats.narration_text: This week's learning focus was the theory behind canary and blue-green deployments — two of the most common strategies for releasing software safely, and how they map directly onto Cloud Run's revision model.

props.topic: CANARY DEPLOYMENTS · BLUE-GREEN · CLOUD RUN REVISIONS · RISK MANAGEMENT
props.segment: Week 10 Technical Learnings — Deployment Strategy Fundamentals
props.runningText: the shared problem → canary → blue-green → one primitive → choosing between them…
output: how both map onto Cloud Run's revision model

beats.role_note: slide 2 -- all-at-once exposure vs. controlled exposure
beats.narration_text: The core problem both strategies address is the same: a standard deploy exposes 100% of users to a new version the instant it goes live, which means any issue is immediately a full-scale incident. Canary and blue-green deployments exist to reduce that exposure before it becomes a problem.

nodes.d: 100% exposure immediately — any issue is a full-scale incident
canary and blue-green both reduce that exposure first

props.caption: Same problem, two different answers — both reduce exposure before it becomes an incident.

beats.role_note: slide 3 -- gradual traffic ramp, monitored at each step
beats.narration_text: A canary deployment releases a new version to a small subset of users, then gradually increases that share while monitoring error rates and performance. The name comes from the idea of a canary in a coal mine — a small, early signal that something is wrong before it affects everyone.

nodes.d: a small subset — the early signal
full rollout, only after each step validates clean

props.caption: A canary in a coal mine — a small, early signal before it affects everyone.

beats.role_note: slide 4 -- two full environments, atomic cutover
beats.narration_text: A blue-green deployment keeps two complete versions running simultaneously — the current version and the new one — and validates the new version in isolation before switching all traffic over in one atomic move. It trades gradual exposure for a cleaner, all-or-nothing cutover with a clear rollback point.

nodes.d: validated in isolation — zero live traffic yet
all traffic switches to green at once

props.caption: Trades gradual exposure for a cleaner cutover with a clear rollback point.

beats.act: WHY CLOUD RUN MAKES BOTH EASY
beats.role_note: slide 5 -- one primitive, two usage patterns
beats.narration_text: What makes both strategies practical here is that Cloud Run already treats each deploy as an immutable revision with controllable traffic percentages. Canary and blue-green aren't separate features to build — they're just two different ways of using the same underlying primitive: multiple revisions existing at once, with traffic deliberately controlled between them.

nodes.d: Cloud Run's own deploy model, already in place
two usage patterns of it, not separate features

props.caption: Nothing new to build — both patterns are just different uses of one existing primitive.

beats.role_note: slide 6 -- which strategy fits which situation
beats.narration_text: Canary deployments are well-suited when you want real traffic to validate a change gradually and automatically limit the blast radius of a problem. Blue-green deployments are well-suited when you want a fully isolated validation before committing, with a single clean moment of cutover. Many teams use both, depending on the type of change.

nodes.d: real traffic validates gradually, limits blast radius
fully isolated validation, one clean cutover
the choice depends on the type of change

props.caption: Not a competition — each fits a different kind of risk to manage.

beats.role_note: slide 7 -- the closing line, Claude cream skin
beats.narration_text: The real takeaway is that these strategies aren't about automation for its own sake — they are deliberate risk management, and understanding the primitive underneath them is what makes it possible to apply either one, or design a new pattern entirely, when the situation calls for it.

artifactLines: The shared problem: a standard deploy exposes 100% of users the instant it goes live.
Canary: a gradual traffic ramp, monitored at each step — an early signal before it affects everyone.
Blue-green: two full environments, validated in isolation, one atomic cutover.
Both are just two usage patterns of Cloud Run's one primitive — immutable revisions + traffic control.
Understanding that primitive is what lets you apply either one, or design a new pattern entirely.
